name: PT Bukit Asam (Persero) Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bukit Asam: a new export channel, the same reserve value
frontmatter.summary: We keep BUY after PTBA's nine-month results and after Indonesia mandated that all coal exports run through state exporter PT DSI from January 2027. The channel change touches nearly half the book but not our model: DSI states it takes no margin, PTBA is aligning its systems and existing contracts continue. The unquantified service fee and a possible go-live slip are what we monitor; the dividend anchor stays our caution.
thesis: The nine-month surge is a price-and-cost story, not a volume recovery: profit more than trebled on a higher average selling price and almost flat cost of revenue while sales and production both fell.
We take this year's volume at the nine-month delivery and then hold the company's own plan rather than import a second downward judgment; the long-run capacity and the reserve base are unchanged.

The realised ratio is now the one the nine-month print measures, not a haircut; it applies to a benchmark above the level it was measured on, and the compression unwinds to the last-actual calibration from the third forecast year.

The new export-channel rule is an administrative change to nearly half the book, not a modelled price or volume cut: DSI states it takes no margin, PTBA is aligning its systems and existing contracts continue; the unquantified service fee and a possible go-live slip are what we monitor.

The life-of-asset DCF at the coal deck's through-cycle path still values the equity well above the price, while the dividend-capacity anchor sits below it; that gap is our honest caution, not a reason to cut the rating.

Cash conversion flatters the nine months: the first half generated more operating cash than the full nine months, so the third quarter absorbed cash while profit rose — we flag the swing and do not call the print clean.

catalysts.event: Fourth-quarter delivery against the full-year sales target after a weak nine months
Decision on the share buyback under review since October 2026
Go-live of the single export channel through state exporter PT DSI
2027 RKAB approval and the national production ceiling
Annual GMS and FY2026 dividend determination

blocks.text: We keep our **BUY** rating and the twelve-month target of **Rp5,112**, an expected total return of **80.0%** from the last close of Rp3,060 [S0, S11]. This note answers a policy event, not a new print; the assumptions of the nine-month update stand, and the life-of-asset DCF still values the equity at Rp5,126 a share [S0, S5, S6].

The new item is the export channel. From 1 January 2027 coal, palm oil and ferro-alloy exports may be handled only by the state exporter PT DSI, under PP 24/2026 and its implementing trade regulation; registered-exporter permits run only to the end of 2026, and through the transition exporters keep their permits but must file contracts, shipment documents and data with DSI [S12]. The regulation's transition article sets out that reporting duty [S14]. The change touches the export half of PTBA's book: exports were 48.5% of nine-month volume, sold to Bangladesh, Vietnam, India, Cambodia and Thailand [S11]. It changes who handles the export documents, not the sales contract — the government says existing contracts continue [S15]. DSI states it does not take a margin and will charge only a service fee, whose size is not published [S16], and PTBA says it is aligning electronic reporting with customs and the DSI platform while asking for clear procedures and contract terms [S13]. We therefore load no fee and cut no volume; inventing either would be an unsourced change. The risk we do carry is timing: the industry association warns that if the permit handover is treated as paperwork, coal may not be exportable on the first day [S12]. That is a first-quarter risk to the export half, set out in the risks and monitoring sections, not a base-case number.

What the nine months changed. The print is a large earnings beat and a clear volume miss. Net profit reached IDR4,410.0bn, revenue IDR35,200.0bn and EBITDA IDR7,190.0bn, with the average selling price up 18.0% and cost of revenue almost flat at IDR27,940.0bn, while sales fell to 32.23 Mt and production to 34.41 Mt [S11]. The profit surge is price-led and cost-disciplined, not the volume recovery the company's plan assumed, and we treat it that way.

What the nine-month update changed in the model. Three inputs moved then, each sourced to the print. First, the delivery path: nine-month sales of 32.23 Mt leave the 49.51 Mt full-year target out of reach without a fourth quarter far above anything delivered this year, so this year takes the delivery rate at 44.00 Mt; from next year we hold the company's own plan — the release reaffirms it and reports production recovering in the third quarter — at 49.50 Mt and 49.50 Mt, the company's own plan rather than a second haircut, with the approved capacity left to the bull [S7, S11]. Second, the realised ratio: the print fixes it. The disclosed nine-month revenue of IDR35,200.0bn over 32.23 Mt of sales, against the coal deck's nine-month Newcastle average translated at the deck's rupiah, gives 0.47; the ratio interpolates to 0.50 next year and returns to the last-actual calibration of 0.52 from the third forecast year [S0, S5, S11]. Third, the cost split: we take the measured strip ratio of 5.63 — the nine-month actual of 5.59 against the company's target — and re-derive the non-mining cost per tonne so the full-year total still ties to the nine-month run-rate, with the fuel inflation of 36.0% carried by the model's fuel link [S11]. No value comes from the horizon: the engine's life-end test stops the DCF well before it, so the horizon setting changes nothing we claim [S5, S7].

We withdraw the reverse-DCF variant view this round. The engine's whole-path override does not reproduce the coal deck's long-run escalation — an identity multiplier flattens the years after the explicit forecast — so any multiplier solved against it sits off the base path; that is an engine issue, escalated to the owner, and we will restore the reverse DCF when the engine reproduces the base. Instead we compare the target with our own scenarios: it sits above the base-scenario value of Rp4,622 and below the bull of Rp9,370, and the bull contributes a little under half of the probability-weighted target [S0, S5].

The honest caution is better documented now. The realised ratio compressed as the benchmark rallied, the volume plan is running short, and the dividend-capacity anchor of Rp3,370 a share sits -34.3% against the DCF because it capitalises near-term earnings and the payout, not the reserve [S5, S6, S11]. We carry that gap in the scenarios.

Bukit Asam is one of the oldest coal enterprises in the archipelago, its Tanjung Enim pits worked
since the colonial era and nationalised after independence. Indonesian thermal coal is a seaborne
swing-supply industry: the country is among the world's largest exporters, its product is mostly
medium-calorific, and its domestic power fleet consumes a mandated share of national output at
administered prices. Calorific content, transport distance and the government reference price, not
company branding, set what a tonne earns.

PTBA is an integrated Indonesian coal company, mining open-pit thermal coal around Tanjung Enim in South Sumatra with smaller operations elsewhere, and running coal transport and port infrastructure alongside the mines [S7]. Its product slate runs from a low-calorific product to a high-calorific one, with the bulk of the blend in the medium grade, represented in our model by a calorific value of 4,600 kcal/kg [S7]. It also carries downstream, power and green-business arms and holds its producing permits as IUP Operasi Produksi, with the Tanjung Enim Air Laya block under a permit dated 2020 [S7].

Sales are split between the domestic market, which took 51.5% of nine-month volume, and exports to Bangladesh, Vietnam, India, Cambodia and Thailand [S11]; from January 2027 that export book must clear through the state exporter PT DSI [S12]. The company's advantage is integration: mine-mouth rail and two dedicated coal ports give it a lower delivered cost than a mine without its own corridor, the moat that lets a medium-calorific producer earn a margin [S7]. Its weakness is product quality and a thin per-tonne margin at trough prices.

Volume grew in the last full year, with production and purchases of 47.19 Mt and sales of 45.43 Mt, but the current year has reversed: nine-month production was 34.41 Mt and sales 32.23 Mt, both below the prior year, with transport volume down further at 27.08 Mt [S7, S11]. Management attributes the earnings growth to production recovery in the third quarter, a stronger sales mix and cost discipline, and still guides to a full-year target near fifty million tonnes [S11]. A share buyback has been under review since October 2026, with no regulatory disclosure yet; we treat it as a catalyst, not as value [S2].

Indonesia's thermal-coal industry is a large, export-led swing supplier with a policy-managed domestic market. National production fell to 790 Mt in the last full year, and the government manages supply through the annual work-and-budget plan: most of the 2026 quota was approved at an aggregate level near the prior-year run-rate after an earlier proposal to tighten it sharply [S7, S9, S10]. PTBA's own plan was approved without a volume cut, but the nine months show that permits and execution are separate constraints [S3, S11].

The domestic-market obligation requires producers to sell a fixed share of output domestically, with a standing US$70/t nominal ceiling on power-station coal in the reviewed coal deck [S0]. It binds in the base case from about FY2042E as the deck's benchmark rises through it, on the power-station part of the domestic book we model; at the full domestic share it is the bear case. The royalty regime is the other structural lever: as an IUP holder PTBA pays the progressive production royalty, banded on the government's coal reference price and higher on higher-calorific tonnage, but its actual book mixes grades and domestic and export tonnes, so the effective rate it pays is the blended one we model [S5, S6].

The export channel is a further structural lever. Under PP 24/2026 and Permendag 15/2026, strategic-resource exports — coal, palm oil and ferro-alloy — may be handled only by the state exporter PT DSI from 1 January 2027; registered-exporter permits lapse at the end of 2026, and during the transition exporters keep their own permits but must report export documents, sales contracts and shipment data to DSI through an integrated system [S12, S14]. The government says existing export contracts continue, and DSI states it takes no margin and will charge a service fee for services such as export inspection, although the enabling regulation lets it set a margin it judges reasonable [S15, S16]. For PTBA, whose exports were 48.5% of nine-month volume [S11], this moves the export paperwork rather than the commercial contract — unless the fee becomes a levy or the handover slips. The industry association's concern is the second: if the permit transition is treated as administration, coal may not be exportable on the first day [S12].

Competitive position. PTBA is a mid-tier national producer by volume and a top-tier holder of reserves, with a reserve base the annual report puts in the billions of tonnes across its permits [S7]. Its integration along rail and port is the moat, but the same integration makes it capital-heavy and exposes it to rail and port availability — transport volume falling faster than sales in the nine months is a reminder that the corridor itself can be the constraint [S11]. Five forces: supplier power moderate, buyer power high because the domestic fleet is mandated and price-capped, substitutes rising slowly, entry barred by permits, rivalry intense in the seaborne market [S7].

The commodity frame. The house coal deck prices Newcastle f.o.b. through a mean-reverting path, with a war-premium year folding back toward a long-run marker well below spot, and the government reference price following it down [S0]. The macro desk's rupiah view is mildly weakening, which translates dollar coal revenue into more rupiah against a rupiah cost base [S0]. Both frame the valuation; we do not re-forecast them.

Actual against forecast. The nine months delivered revenue of IDR35,200.0bn, reported EBITDA of IDR7,190.0bn and net profit of IDR4,410.0bn [S11]. Two definitions have to be separated before the print is set against the forecast. The release's EBITDA is the company's own measure and is consistent with including the associate contribution of IDR581.3bn [S11]; our model's EBITDA is an operating measure — operating profit plus depreciation and amortisation — and excludes associates, which we carry below the line. On that reading the nine-month operating EBITDA is IDR7,190.0bn less the IDR581.3bn associate share, and the full-year forecast of IDR11,156.1bn is struck on the operating basis too, so the comparison is like for like [S0, S5, S11]. Net profit bridges the same way: nine-month IDR4,410.0bn less the first half's IDR2,643.4bn leaves the third quarter's contribution, and our full-year forecast of IDR7,629.6bn implies a fourth quarter materially above that third-quarter pace, not near it [S6, S11].

The fourth-quarter step-up is arithmetic from an annual build, not a second quarterly forecast, and it is anchored on the two measured inputs rather than on a margin assumption. The full-year volume 44.00 Mt is the nine months plus the prior-year fourth-quarter delivery pace; the realised ratio 47.1% is the one the nine-month print measures — nine-month revenue over sales against the deck's nine-month benchmark translated at the deck's rupiah — and it is applied to the deck's full-year benchmark of 137.00 [S0, S11]. That full-year benchmark itself embeds the deck's fourth-quarter forward price, which sits above the nine-month average, so the implied fourth-quarter selling price is the deck forward at the same measured ratio; it is the forward that lifts the quarter, not a wider margin [S0]. Filling the nine months from the print therefore loads that price uplift into the residual quarter, and because the cost base is held flat in nominal terms through the explicit years most of it falls through to profit. Holding the fourth quarter at the nine-month price instead would leave the year below the deck's own path, which is not the most-likely reading; the signpost is whether the deck's forward is realised [S0, S11]. The identical statement is in the assumptions file, so the build and the report cannot drift.

The mix of the beat matters more than its size. Revenue rose on sales that fell to 32.23 Mt because the average selling price rose 18.0%, against a high-calorific benchmark that rose more; cost of revenue rose only marginally to IDR27,940.0bn as the strip ratio fell to 5.59 and the company held operating costs; and the profit line also benefited from lower finance costs of IDR136.5bn and associate income of IDR581.3bn [S11]. The lift from associates and the lower finance cost are below-the-line items the DCF does not capitalise.

The model's finance charge is above the nine-month run-rate, and that is a basis difference rather than a forecast of dearer debt. The engine applies the three-year historical cost of debt to gross debt, which now includes the low-coupon back-to-back facility secured by the export-proceeds placements, while the income earned on those placements sits outside the modelled cash balance [S6, S11]. We take no value from the gap in either direction; it is a small caution inside the target, and the nine-month net finance position is the better read of the year [S11].

Cash conversion is the flag the nine-month aggregate hides. First-half operating cash flow was IDR4,625.7bn [S6] against IDR4,440.0bn for the nine months [S11], so the third quarter absorbed operating cash while profit rose from IDR2,643.4bn in the first half to IDR4,410.0bn for the nine months [S6, S11]. That is a one-quarter working-capital and receivables swing of roughly the size of the quarter's profit. The release does not decompose it, so we do not clear the print: we cannot tell from the summary whether it is receivables, tax timing or the export-proceeds placement, so we treat it as a working-capital swing and watch it at the full-year accounts; the realised-price and royalty data do not point to a revenue-recognition issue [S6, S11].

The last full year was a thin-margin year, and the restatement still drives it: revenue of IDR42,651.7bn, EBITDA of IDR5,222.2bn after the audited depreciation and amortisation charge of IDR2,014.1bn replaces the data pack's fragment, and royalties of IDR4,322.7bn, about a tenth of coal revenue [S5]. The effective royalty rate is the one we carry into the forecast, consistent with the interim accounts and with the nine-month release's nearly flat cost of revenue [S5, S6, S11].

The balance sheet remains strong but its shape changed. At the end of September cash was IDR4,890.0bn and bank loans IDR4,210.0bn, the latter including a back-to-back facility secured by export-proceeds placements [S11]. Those placements sit in the investing outflow of IDR3,500.0bn, outside cash and equivalents [S11]; netting the placements against the loans leaves net liquid assets close to the June balance sheet, so the operating move carries no separate bridge item [S6]. The bridge is struck on the June balance sheet, and that balance sheet carries the FY2025 dividend payable of IDR1,304.8bn — the dividend declared 11 June 2026 and paid 10 July 2026 [S6]. Cash owed to shareholders is not equity value, so the bridge deducts it; net cash attributable to equity is that much lower than the market block's reading: the deduction is the dividend payable itself, IDR1,304.8bn, taken before the equity value is struck. The equity-accounted stakes are untouched at book [S6].

Forecasts. We take the delivery rate for the first forecast year and hold the company's plan thereafter, holding unit costs flat in nominal terms through FY2030E and escalating them with Indonesian inflation after that, with dollar prices escalating on US inflation — the nominal-consistent treatment the house method requires [S0]. We say flat in nominal, not in real terms: at Indonesian inflation the explicit years carry a gentle real decline, which is the more optimistic reading and is the one the model actually holds. The realised ratio keeps the 2026 compression in the first year and returns to the last-actual calibration thereafter, so the long-run value is not set by a forecast-year spike or trough [S5, S11]. Capital spending is set to the company's IDR3,640.0bn budget for the year — the per-tonne rate plus a budget top-up — rather than the lower volume-times-rate figure, so committed project spend is not cut by the volume miss; the difference is a fraction of the per-share DCF of Rp5,126 [S11].

The forecast peaks with the deck's near-term price years and reverts with the benchmark, but the terminal years are not a reserve-life perpetuity: the DMO ceiling clips the capped power-station tonnes from about FY2042E — it is the reviewed coal deck's policy assumption, held flat in nominal terms with no escalation [S0] — so free cash flow fades before the reserve is exhausted and the life-end test stops the DCF at FY2057E rather than at the reserve year. There is no terminal growth rate: the DCF runs on reserves and stops when marginal value turns negative. The excluded tail is a modelling convention, not a forecast, which is why the bull lifts the ceiling with the benchmark so the capped tonnes stay economic; that cap lift is a real difference between the base and the bull, and the base does not pay for an administrative price rise the state has not made [S0].

Why this method set. PTBA is a life-of-asset commodity producer, so the primary method is a life-of-reserve DCF at the coal deck's through-cycle prices, not a spot multiple. Valuing a cyclical on current-year earnings is the classic procyclical error; the NAV uses the deck's mean-reverting path, and the other anchors are secondary — real weight, but a minority of it. The house weighting is 60% to the life DCF, 25% to EV/EBITDA and 15% to dividend capacity [S5, S6].
Cost of capital.

The build uses the risk-free rate from the house macro deck, the mature-market equity premium and Indonesia's country risk premium, an unlevered beta from the industry regression median (0.80) re-levered for the group's small net debt, and a dollar cost of debt; the resulting weighted average cost of capital is 11.2%, applied to the reserve-life cash flows [S5, S6].
Primary method.

The DCF discounts free cash flow to the firm over the reserve life, adds the June-2026 net cash after deducting the dividend payable of IDR1,304.8bn [S6], brings in the equity-accounted investments of IDR10,713.4bn at book, and deducts minorities. That book is not a black box: most of it is HBAP, the South Sumatra mine-mouth power venture selling to PLN under a long-term purchase agreement, carried at IDR7,700.4bn against venture net assets of IDR17,111.9bn; BPI, the Lahat mine-mouth plant, at IDR2,927.2bn against IDR4,899.1bn; and a small rail venture at IDR5.4bn [S6]. The carrying values are the group's equity-method share of net assets, and the interim accounts disclose no impairment or pending review, so we treat book as the LK's own measure of recoverable value rather than an independent mark; on the nine-month associate run-rate of IDR581.3bn the total implies a low-to-mid-teens earnings multiple, which is what a depreciation-heavy, PPA-backed power asset looks like on earnings, not evidence the stake is overstated [S6]. The HBAP shares are pledged to the export-import bank that funded the project — a structure point we note rather than price [S6]. One definitional note: the modelled FY2025A net-debt history excludes the current maturities of long-term bank borrowings, which is why it sits a little below a leaf-by-leaf rebuild of the December balance sheet; the valuation bridge is struck on the June-2026 balance sheet, which reconciles exactly, so the exclusion carries no value effect [S6]. It carries no terminal value because the reserves are finite. The engine's life-end test stops the DCF at the point of maximum cumulative value. In the base case the stop is set by the fixed nominal DMO ceiling clipping the capped tonnes from about FY2042E, so the DCF does not run to the full reserve year, and the long tail of a very large reserve base is not counted when it would subtract value [S0, S7]. The life the DCF runs rests on the permits as much as on the reserve: the nearest producing permit, Banko Barat, runs only to 9 April 2027 — just inside the next financial year — with Muara Tiga Besar to 29 August 2029 and Air Laya to 31 December 2030, so FY2027E volume itself depends on a renewal falling inside the forecast year; the annual report says the company renews its IUPs on time but discloses no application yet [S7]. Discounting at the cost of capital, roughly three-fifths of the DCF's present value sits in the years after the flagship permit's current term ends, so renewal is the largest single assumption in the valuation, not a footnote — a reader who does not accept timely renewal should not accept most of the target [S0, S7].
Cross-checks.

The EV/EBITDA anchor applies a blend of the peer median and PTBA's own five-year average, 5.50x, to the last actual year's EBITDA of IDR5,222.2bn, giving an anchor -28.3% against the primary DCF [S5, S6]. We name the metric plainly because FY2025A is a trough: the same multiple on the forecast year's IDR11,156.1bn would land above the DCF, so the gap is cycle position, not an asset-value signal, and we do not read it as the reserve being overvalued. The dividend-capacity anchor capitalises the modelled distribution at the sector's yield — the anchor the market most often uses for Indonesian coal names — and it lands -34.3% against the DCF. The dividend anchor is the lower of the two and the gap widened with the nine-month update, and we explain it rather than assert a band: it capitalises a distribution of Rp398 a share struck on earnings that carry the compressed 2026 realised ratio, while the life-of-reserve DCF runs the deck's full price path over the whole reserve life. These two are not footnotes: they carry 25.0% and 15.0% of the target, and both divergences are about where in the price cycle each method looks, not about the asset; the house weights favour the DCF [S5, S7].

Sensitivity. We withhold the benchmark-and-rupiah grid this round. Every grid that shocks the benchmark runs through the engine's whole-path override, which flattens the deck's post-explicit escalation, so the centre cell does not reconcile with the target and we will not publish a table we cannot stand behind [S0]. The engine's volume-and-cost-intensity grid does not touch the benchmark, is clean, and its centre reproduces the base value, so the ranking below rests on a run we can defend [S0]. The rank order is unchanged: a life-of-reserve value is most sensitive to the realised price and the rupiah, and least to volume at the margin — an inventory-of-reserves business, not a growth business [S0, S5]. The one judgement the price grids do not settle is how much of the domestic book sits under the cap. We charge it to the power-station share, hold that share in both tails, and let the scenarios move the cap level instead; the FY2025 accounts identify the PLN group as the only customer above a tenth of revenue at IDR14,429.2bn [S5, S11]. A higher power share than our mid-point would lower the capped tonnage's realisation and the value, and the sensitivity is bounded on both sides by the tails' cap cut and lift rather than by a second grid.

Royalty tail. The base charges the LK's effective rate flat through the whole path, which is the most-likely rate for a domestic-heavy, mixed-calorific book that pays a blended rate today. The schedule is progressive, though, and the deck's tail benchmark is far above today's, so the flat rate could understate the royalty in the late years. Running the deck's mid-band IUP schedule on the HBA reference instead of the flat rate — the conservative tail test — lowers the life DCF by roughly a tenth from Rp5,126 [S0]. We do not carry it in the base because no observed year charges that band, and the interim accounts show the same blended rate; the sensitivity is disclosed so a reader who expects the tail to be taxed at the schedule can see the cost. The bull is not credited with the banded schedule, so the flat rate flatters the bull rather than the base if the tail is wrong [S5, S6].

What the price implies. We do not publish a reverse-DCF multiplier this round, for the same engine reason: a multiplier solved on the flattened path is not on the base path [S0]. The directional reading does not depend on the grid, and it is stated plainly: at Rp3,060 the market prices the equity at about three-fifths of the life-of-reserve DCF of Rp5,126, so it is discounting well over a third of the base path before any probability weighting [S0, S5]. We will restore the reverse DCF — the implied benchmark price that today's price supports — as soon as the engine reproduces the deck's long-run path; until then this ratio is the substitute. The target is above the base-scenario value of Rp4,622 and below the bull of Rp9,370, and the market price of Rp3,060 sits between the bear-scenario value of Rp1,834 and the base, much closer to the bear: the market is assigning materially more weight to the downside state than the quarter we carry, and the gap to our base is a probability disagreement rather than a different view of the reserve value [S5, S6]. Calibration note: re-pricing the last actual year at its own benchmark, volume, realised ratio and rupiah reproduces the LK's EBITDA to within a couple of per cent, with the residual carried by the cost split, which is struck on the nine-month run-rate and the current fuel basis; the engine's headline gap is wider because it prices FY2025A's volume and benchmark at the FY2026E realised ratio and rupiah [S5, S11].
Downside risks, with our view of likelihood and impact.

items: **Commodity price (high likelihood, high impact).** The benchmark reverting through the deck's
long-run marker below spot is the base case, and a deeper oversupply — Chinese and Indian restarts,
relaxed Indonesian supply discipline — takes realised prices below our path. The per-tonne margin is
thin at trough prices, so small price moves are large earnings moves [S0].
**Realisation compression (high likelihood, medium impact).** The nine-month record shows the
medium-calorific book captured much less of the benchmark rally than the high-calorific index, so
the compression we now carry could persist beyond the next year rather than unwind [S11].
**Volume execution (high likelihood, high impact).** Nine-month sales ran well below the plan and
transport volumes fell faster, so the recovery we assume is a forecast, not a delivered fact; a
repeat of the first nine months removes the second-half volume the plan needs [S11].
**Domestic policy and quota (medium likelihood, high impact).** A tightened RKAB ceiling, or a
domestic-market obligation applied at a lower price, would cut volume or realisation. PTBA's own
RKAB was approved without a cut, but national policy has swung before [S9, S10].
**Export-channel transition (medium likelihood, medium impact).** From January 2027 every export
tonne must clear through PT DSI; exports were 48.5% of nine-month volume, so a go-live
slip stops the export half, and a service fee takes a slice of realised price. As arithmetic: each
point of fee is charged on 48.5% of the forecast revenue of
IDR50,627.2bn, with the after-tax profit and DCF effect following in proportion —
small per point, but a levy on nearly half the book. We carry no fee in any case because no rate is
published: the bear is deliberately fee-free and this sensitivity is the substitute [S16]. The
industry association warns the permit handover could halt shipments on day one, and the enabling
regulation lets DSI set a margin it judges reasonable [S12, S16]; the bear's volume cut carries
that stoppage, as set out below. PTBA says it is aligning its systems and asks for clear
procedures [S13].
**Currency (medium likelihood, medium impact).** A sharply stronger rupiah compresses the dollar
revenue translated into rupiah while the cost base stays in rupiah; the reverse is the tailwind in
our forecast [S0].
**Cost inflation (medium likelihood, medium impact).** Fuel prices rose 36.0% in the nine
months and offset the lower strip ratio; a sustained fuel price or a higher strip ratio as pits
deepen would raise cash cost per tonne [S11].
**Working capital (medium likelihood, medium impact).** The third quarter absorbed operating cash
while profit rose; a repeat would turn the earnings beat into a receivables story and cut the
dividend the capacity anchor capitalises [S6, S11].
**Governance and related parties (low likelihood, medium impact).** A state-controlled issuer with a
majority related-party revenue book carries the modal Indonesian value-destruction risk; the flows
are disclosed and priced off third-party terms, but they are large [S5, S7].

blocks.text: Scenarios.

Bear: the state takes a larger share of a state-owned producer — a work-and-budget cut toward the lower national ceiling the government proposed before approving the higher one, or a tighter domestic-market obligation at the capped power price — while the benchmark rolls back through the deck's long-run marker and the medium-calorific book keeps the realised price a fifth weaker on the company's own ratio, so the whole price path, escalation included, moves down with it. Volume is cut about five million tonnes below the base, the price cap is cut a fifth below the deck's level — the mirror of the bull's lift — so the fixed nominal ceiling clips the capped tonnes harder and the payout falls to the FY2025 trough ratio as earnings fall. That volume cut carries the January handover too: a quarter's export tonnage lost at go-live sits inside the five million tonnes, so the policy event is in the number rather than beside it [S12]. The volume risk is visible in the actuals: the nine months ran below the plan, so the bear is a continuation of what has been delivered, not a hypothesis [S9, S10, S11]. Bull: a sustained war-premium holds the benchmark above the long-run marker and the realised price is shocked a fifth above the base path — the mirror of the bear's cut, and a scenario boundary rather than a claim that the ratio returns to an observed level, because the three published years do not bound a tail — as the medium-calorific spread narrows and the export share rises [S5, S11]. The price cap is lifted a fifth with the benchmark here — the mirror of the bear's cut — so the capped tonnes stay economic a little longer, and the payout returns to the boom-year ratio PTBA's own record demonstrates. Volume adds only half a million tonnes because the base already runs at the company's plan level from the third year, so the add reaches the approved capacity exactly — a larger bull would be above the RKAB ceiling — and the upside is carried on realised price, the mirror cap lift and payout, not on above-capacity tonnes [S7, S11]. The two tails now shock the same four drivers — realised price, the DMO cap, payout and volume — with mirrored moves on the first three; the volume asymmetry is the only one, and it is sourced: the bear continues the delivered nine-month shortfall while the bull is bounded by the approved capacity. The full reserve-tail unlock from a doubled cap is not paid here: run on its own it adds a low-single-digit percentage to the bull's value and was the source of the one-tailed target the prior round carried, so it sits in the sensitivity discussion instead [S0]. The bear's capped-share widening and its cap cut land almost the same value, which is why the mirror is the honest construction.

The target is above our own base scenario but now below the primary DCF. At the house probabilities the bull contributes the largest single share of the weighted target on its quarter weight — realised price and payout do most of that work, with the mirrored cap lift a minor increment — with the base a similar share and the bear the remainder; the bull carries Rp9,370 against the base of Rp4,622, so the rating leans on a state in which the realised ratio and the payout recover and the price holds [S5, S8]. We consider that state as likely as the bear, which is why the target sits above the base; after the scenario mirror it sits just below the primary DCF of Rp5,126 rather than above it, so no part of the target any longer rests on an administrative-price rise the state has not made [S0]. It is a probability-weighted number, not a base-case number, and it sits below the bull.

The optionality the base case does not pay for. The bull now carries the higher payout, which is how we quantify the distribution optionality rather than asserting it: a payout back at the boom-year ratio flows straight into the dividend-capacity anchor and is worth the bull's Rp9,370 against the base [S7, S8]. The buyback itself stays outside both tails: it is under board review with no regulatory disclosure, so its size, timing and price are unknown and a share-count cut would be invented; the decision that would make it value is a filed buyback struck below the DCF of Rp5,126 [S2]. Beyond the reserve base we value, the annual report carries a resource inventory roughly twice the proved-and-probable reserve, including a large un-developed block at Banko Tengah; converting even part of it extends the modelled life rather than changing near-term cash flows, so we treat it as upside prose, not value [S7].

Signposts that would change our view: the realised ratio recovering while the benchmark rolls over; a formal buyback or higher dividend policy; an RKAB cut applied to PTBA itself; a rupiah break either way; delivered volume close to the full-year plan; any sign of a lower domestic price; and a DSI service fee that becomes a material levy on export revenue, or an export stoppage at go-live [S2, S8, S10, S11, S12, S16].

Ownership and control. PTBA is state-controlled: the government holds the special Dwiwarna share and the MIND ID mining holding owns 65.9% of the register, with the public holding the balance and a small treasury position [S7]. Strategy follows the holding's direction, and major corporate actions need board and shareholder approval — the structure that governs the buyback now under review [S2, S7].

Related parties. Related-party revenue is large because state entities are related parties under the Indonesian accounting standards; the audited note puts coal revenue from related parties at a majority of coal sales in the last actual year [S5]. This is a disclosure-quality point rather than a red flag — the flows are to the domestic power fleet and other state buyers — but we do not take arm's length on trust, because the same state sets both the domestic price ceiling and the reference price that bands the royalty. The test we apply is whether the blended realised price the company actually achieves sits below the government reference price for its calorific band: the nine-month record shows the realised price below the contemporaneous benchmark and the royalty charged at the blended schedule rate, which is what arm's-length state pricing under the domestic-market rules looks like [S5, S6, S11]. The company states it has no material conflict-of-interest transactions [S7]. The reclamation and mine-closure obligation is a balance-sheet provision and is reflected in the accounts; it is not an incremental DCF charge because the life-end test truncates the model ahead of reserve exhaustion [S5, S6].

Audit and reporting. The last full year's consolidated statements carry an unmodified opinion from KAP Purwantono, Susanti dan Surja, a member firm of Ernst & Young Global, with no special GMS status, going-concern notation or qualification [S5]. The nine-month release is an unaudited press summary, so we weight the audited annual figures and expect the usual fourth-quarter true-ups [S11].

Dividends. The stated policy is to distribute at least a set share of net profit under the IPO prospectus unless the GMS decides otherwise, with a long record of paying above that floor [S7]. The FY2025 book dividend was approved at the June-2026 annual GMS at IDR1,310.0bn, a payout well above the policy floor but below the boom-year payouts [S7, S8]. Our modelled payout sits between the floor and that record, and the stronger 2026 earnings lift the modelled distribution to Rp398 a share [S8, S11].

ESG exposures. PTBA's material issues are land and biodiversity around the Tanjung Enim and Kalimantan pits, mine-closure and reclamation liabilities, water and tailings management, and the transition risk of a thermal-coal franchise. It carries a reclamation and mine-closure provision and reports sustainability and climate disclosures alongside the annual report, and it is a large regional employer running community programmes [S5, S7]. The transition is the structural risk: a net-zero path and the grid's renewables build eventually shrink the domestic thermal market, and the reserve life we value reaches well into that horizon.

Dated catalysts are in the frontmatter: fourth-quarter delivery against target, a buyback decision, the January go-live of the PT DSI export channel, the annual GMS that sets the FY2026 dividend, and the 2027 work-and-budget plan [S2, S8, S10, S11, S12].

Between updates we monitor a short list. First, the price side: the Newcastle benchmark and the government reference price off the coal deck, spot against the deck's path, and the rupiah off the macro deck [S0]. Second, the company's own delivery: quarterly volumes and realised price against the plan and against the ratio we have calibrated, the stripping ratio and the cash cost per tonne against the last actual, and the transport volumes on the Tanjung Enim corridor [S11]. Third, the cash side: the full-year bridge from operating cash flow to profit, after the third-quarter swing [S6, S11]. Fourth, the policy side: the RKAB decision, any change to the domestic-market obligation or the price ceiling, and any royalty-order change [S3, S5, S9, S10]. Fifth, the export channel: the first post-transition clearances after January 2027, the DSI service-fee schedule, any margin determination under PP 24/2026, and whether PTBA's export contracts are novated cleanly [S12, S13, S16].

The number that would move our rating most is the realised price-to-benchmark ratio recovering while the benchmark rolls over: that is the bull case, it is not in the base case, and we would re-underwrite on the first report of it [S5, S7]. The second is a formal buyback or a higher dividend policy, which would lift the dividend-capacity anchor that sits below the DCF [S2, S8].

bear.narrative: Newcastle rolls back through the deck's long-run floor as Chinese and Indian mine restarts and relaxed Indonesian RKAB discipline turn the 2025-26 war-premium tightness into oversupply, and the state takes a larger share of a state-owned producer: an RKAB cut toward the ~600 Mt national level the government proposed before approving ~720 Mt, or a tighter DMO at the capped power price, cuts PTBA's volume by about a tenth while its medium-CV, domestic-heavy blend keeps the realised-to-benchmark ratio compressed as the benchmark falls. The realised price is shocked on the company ratio (0.8x) rather than on the benchmark deck, so the whole price path, including its long-run escalation, moves together. The DMO ceiling is cut a fifth below the reviewed deck level — the mirror of the bull's lift — so the fixed nominal cap bites harder and truncates the modelled life earlier, and the dividend steps down to the FY2025 trough payout as earnings fall. The volume cut also carries the transition risk this update exists to examine: a delayed permit handover at the January 2027 DSI go-live would strand a quarter's export tonnage, about the size of the shock, so the policy event is inside the number rather than beside it [S12]. The bear carries no DSI service fee because no rate is published [S16]; the per-point fee sensitivity sits in the report, not in the scenario.

bull.narrative: A sustained war-premium in seaborne thermal coal and Chinese import curbs keep Newcastle above the deck's long-run marker, and the realised price is shocked a fifth above the base path — the mirror of the bear's cut, which takes the realised-to-benchmark ratio above the FY2025A calibration rather than toward it. That is a scenario boundary, not a forecast of an observed ratio: the three published years (FY2023-25) do not bound a tail, and the ratio can rise without any observed level being contradicted if the medium-CV spread narrows and the export share keeps rising. Production returns to the company's 49.5 Mt plan and the 50 Mt capacity, which caps the volume upside, and the extra dollars convert into cash against a rupiah cost base that does not move with them. The DMO ceiling is lifted a fifth above the reviewed deck's US$70/t level (S0) — the mirror of the bear's cut — so the capped domestic tonnes stay economic a little longer; the full reserve-tail unlock is shown as a sensitivity in the report, not paid in the base. Royalty stays flat at the LK's effective rate in both tails (no scenario switches to the banded schedule), and the higher distribution PTBA's record demonstrates is paid as the payout returns to its FY2023-24 level. The two tails shock the same four drivers — realised price, volume, the DMO cap and payout — with mirrored moves on the price, cap and payout, and the capacity limit on the bull's volume the one sourced asymmetry. That capacity limit is justified in qc_justifications.

assumptions.label: Sales volume plan
assumptions.basis: DATE 2026-10-29 revision. FY2026E is the 9M-2026 delivery rolled to a full year: sales ran 32.23 Mt in the nine months to September (F36, S11) and hitting the 49.51 Mt target (F42) would need a Q4 of 17.28 Mt — 47% above Q4-2025's 11.73 Mt (FY2025 45.43 Mt, F1, less 33.70 Mt in 9M 2025, S11). Q4 at the prior-year pace gives about 44 Mt, so FY2026E is 44.0 Mt. From FY2027E we hold the company's own plan rather than a judgment glide: the 9M release reaffirms production of 49.55 Mt and sales of 49.51 Mt (F42, S11) and reports production recovering in Q3, so FY2027E is 49.5 Mt, the last sourced forward level, and FY2028E onward holds 49.5 Mt — the company's own plan, not a haircut, and below the 50 Mt RKAB-approved capacity (S3, S11) only because the plan is the sourced level. The bull adds half a million tonnes to reach the approved capacity; a larger volume would be above the RKAB ceiling. The 9M shortfall is a 2026 execution miss, not evidence of a permanently lower capability: production fell 4.1% to 34.41 Mt (F37) while the plan was reaffirmed (F42), and the earlier plan basis was management's optimistic delivery guidance (S4). No default haircut is carried into 2027-28.

assumptions.label: Realised price / benchmark
assumptions.basis: DATE 2026-10-29 revision. FY2026E 0.471 is the ratio the 9M-2026 print produces, not a haircut. Numerator: coal revenue is not disclosed for the nine months, so the measurement uses the disclosed 9M revenue of Rp35.20trn (F35, S11) on 32.23 Mt of sales (F36), about Rp1,092,000/t; total revenue includes the small non-coal book (H1 other-activity revenue is Rp357.6bn on F19 less F26), which overstates the coal ASP by about 1.5%, so the true coal ratio sits a shade below 0.471 — still above the 0.4635 previously carried. Denominator: the coal deck's 2026 Newcastle average of about US$131.9/t (Q1 122.3, Q2 135.4, Q3 138.1), translated at the deck's FY2026E rupiah of 17,570: 1,092,000 / (131.9 x 17,570) = 0.471. The release's ASP +18% against Newcastle +25% and ICI-3 +26% (F51, S11) confirms that the medium-CV, 51.5%-domestic book (F50, F15) captured less than the high-CV benchmark. FY2026E applies the ratio to the full-year benchmark of US$137.0, which is 3.8% above the nine-month average because it embeds the Q4 forward curve (149-153, coal deck); at a stable ratio that reproduces the full-year ASP, and no Q4 lag is added. Because the model is annual, filling the nine months from the print loads that 3.8% full-year price uplift into the residual fourth quarter, which is why the implied Q4 profit sits above the third quarter's run-rate — disclosed in report section 3 and consistent with the annual build, not a separate quarterly forecast. DATE 2026-10-31 revision (QC Q2). The Q4 build is now anchored explicitly, not left implicit: FY2026E selling price = the 9M-measured ratio 0.471 x the deck's full-year benchmark (which embeds the Q4 forward 149-153, S0), so the implied Q4 price is that forward at the same measured ratio, not a wider margin. Holding Q4 at the 9M price level instead was the alternative; it would leave the year below the deck's own path and is the cautious, not the most-likely, reading, so it is not used. FY2027E 0.497 interpolates between the 9M observation and the FY2025A calibration 0.5175 at the deck's lower FY2027E benchmark of US$118.0; from FY2028E the model holds the FY2025A calibration (realised Rp922,499/t on 45.43 Mt over the FY2025A Newcastle average of US$108.4/t), the last full actual year, to lt, as the desk rule requires: the last full actual year sets the long-run ratio, and the 2026 compression is the war-premium year unwinding. The drift FY2026E -> lt is +9.9%, below the engine's 10% ratio threshold, so the engine raises no drift flag and no separate justification key is needed. DATE 2026-10-30 update: the single-export-channel rule does not move this ratio. From 1 January 2027 coal exports must run through the state exporter PT DSI under PP 24/2026 and Permendag 15/2026 (S12, S14), but DSI states it does not take a margin and will charge only a service fee whose size is not published (S16), PTBA says it is aligning its electronic reporting with the customs system and the DSI platform (S13), and existing export contracts continue (S15). No fee or haircut is loaded because none is quantified; the fee and the go-live risk sit in the report's risk and monitoring sections (S12, S16).

assumptions.label: Share of volume under a price cap (e.g. DMO)
assumptions.basis: DATE 2026-10-29 revision (QC Q2). 0.27 is half the domestic upper bound, not the upper bound itself: the deck's US$70/t ceiling is a nominal power-station price (d.coal.dmo_cap, lt 70, no escalation) and it is charged only to the power-station part of the book, not to every domestic tonne. Domestic sales were 54% of FY2025 volume (S7 p.65) and 51.5% in 9M-2026 (F50, S11), and the annual report says domestic supply goes "particularly to power plants" (S7) without publishing the split, so the base charges the cap to about half the domestic book (power). The share is held at 0.27 in every scenario: QC Q1 (round 1) showed that moving this share in one tail while the other tail moved the cap level was not a mirror, so both tails now move d.coal.dmo_cap a fifth either way and the share stays put. This is a stated bound-splitting judgement between two no-disclosure endpoints, not a disclosed figure. The realised ratio (calibrated on the FY2025A actual, when the US$70 cap did not bind) already embeds today's domestic power pricing. Not inert: the engine's own run at 0.54 showed the cap biting from FY2042E and truncating the DCF at FY2051E instead of the reserve year.

assumptions.label: Strip ratio (bcm per tonne) or cost-intensity factor
assumptions.basis: DATE 2026-10-29 revision. 5.63x is the company's own 2026 target and the 9M-2026 run-rate: the strip ratio fell from 5.98x to 5.59x in the nine months, against a 5.63x full-year target (F41/F42, S11), not the FY2025A actual of 6.06x (F16). It is the intensity factor that multiplies cost_per_bcm; the cost split is re-derived below so the FY2026E total still ties to the 9M run-rate, with the lower strip intensity offset inside other_cost_unit and the fuel link (fuel prices +36% yoy, F54/S11). No grade or mine-plan drift is asserted.

assumptions.label: Mining cost per bcm (or per unit when intensity is 1)
assumptions.basis: IDR 50,000/bcm (about US$3.0/bcm at the FY2025A rate), the sector norm for Indonesian open-pit overburden removal by contractors — the same US$3.0/bcm the COAL peer set uses. PTBA does not disclose a per-bcm rate, so the split between this and other_cost_unit is a proxy chosen so that strip_ratio x cost_per_bcm plus other_cost_unit lands the FY2025A LK cash cost. Held flat in nominal terms; the engine grows it at the IDR long-run inflation scalar after FY2030E.

assumptions.label: Fuel share of mining cost
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — PTBA does not break out fuel; sector norm retained

assumptions.label: Other cash cost per unit (haul, barge, process)
assumptions.basis: IDR 374,738/t: the balancing item that brings total cash cost to the LK-calibrated level, re-derived for the 5.63x strip ratio. Derivation unchanged: FY2025A cost of revenues Rp36,394,624m (S5 p.128) less royalties to government Rp4,322,659m (F11) less the D&A charged inside cost of revenues (depreciation Rp1,575,007m + amortisation Rp135,726m = Rp1,710,733m, S5 p.128) = Rp30,361,232m of group cash operating cost; the cost of the Rp742,638m of other-activity revenue (F13, S5 Catatan 26) is charged separately on the other_cogs line at Rp668,374m (742,638 x (1 - other_margin)), so the coal cash cost is 30,361,232 - 668,374 = Rp29,692,858m; divided by 45.43 Mt (F1) = Rp653,597/t. The strip component at 5.63x and IDR50,000/bcm is Rp281,500/t, and the fuel uplift at the FY2026E brent of 96.0 (30% fuel share, about +41% against FY2025A) is roughly Rp34,600/t, so other_cost_unit = 690,835 - 281,500 - 34,600 = about Rp374,738/t: the FY2026E total stays at the 9M run-rate while the strip decomposition follows the actual. It carries PTBA's heavy haulage and rail/port cost — the H1-2026 LK shows coal transportation services of Rp3,998,563m as the second-largest cash line inside cost of revenues, behind mining services of Rp5,737,978m (S6 Catatan 27a). Held flat in nominal terms, then grown at IDR inflation. DATE 2026-10-30 update: no PT DSI service fee is loaded into cash cost. PP 24/2026 lets the state export channel set a reasonable margin (S16) but no rate is published, so loading one would be an unsourced cost; the item is monitored, not modelled (S12, S16).

assumptions.label: Royalty rate (flat-regime fallback; not used under tier mode)
assumptions.basis: The LK's effective royalty rate, charged flat on coal revenue. FY2025A: royalties to government Rp4,322,659m (F11, S5 p.128) on coal revenue Rp41,909,086m (F13, S5 p.127) = 10.31%; FY2024A 9.69% (Rp4,077,822m / Rp42,084,008m). The H1-2026 interim confirms it again: Rp2,209,879m of royalties (S6 Catatan 27a) on Rp21,672,370m of coal revenue (S6 Catatan 26) = 10.20%. The owner directive (MOST_LIKELY_BASE_CASE) requires the LK's effective rate in the base case, so the model is flat here rather than applying the top IUP band to every tonne: PTBA sells 54% of its volume domestically (S7 p.65) off a 2,800-6,100 GAR slate (F15), so its book mixes the low and mid tranches of the PP 19/2025 schedule and the blended paid rate is the most-likely one. All three scenarios keep this flat effective rate: none switches royalty_mode or the schedule, so the bull is not credited with the banded schedule — at its higher realised price the top band would tax coal revenue above the flat rate, so if the flat rate biases the bull at all it flatters it.

assumptions.label: Other revenue
assumptions.basis: FY2025A other revenue of Rp742,638m = total revenue Rp42,651,724m less coal revenue Rp41,909,086m (F13, S5) — trading, transport, palm and services across PTBA's subsidiaries (S7). Held flat in nominal terms and escalated at IDR inflation beyond FY2030E.

assumptions.label: Gross margin on other revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default constant

assumptions.label: D&A per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: IDR 44,334/t = the LK's own consolidated depreciation AND amortisation of Rp2,014,102m in FY2025 (F7, S5 p.159, segment additional disclosures) divided by 45.43 Mt (F1). This is the RESTATEMENT the desk rule demands: the data pack's D&A of Rp300,136m is only ~15% of the real charge, because the IDX direct cash-flow presentation carries no D&A line and the pack picked up a fragment. The segment note is the anchor because PTBA's mine-property depletion is amortised on a unit-of-production basis inside cost of revenues and is not in the income-statement depreciation line. Held flat in real terms, then escalated at IDR inflation.

assumptions.label: Sustaining capex per unit (reporting currency)
assumptions.basis: IDR 77,159/t = FY2025A capital expenditure of Rp3,505,367m (F9, S5 p.20 cash-flow statement, "perolehan aset tetap dan tanaman produktif") divided by 45.43 Mt (F1). FY2025 was an investment peak — FY2024 capex was Rp1,231,886m (F10), about IDR 28,700/t on that year's volume — because the Tanjung Enim-Kramasan coal-transport project and the downstream/power build ran through the year (S7). We use the last actual, as the rule requires, and flag that it is the top of the recent range in §3 and the sensitivity table; no drifts are asserted.

assumptions.label: Other capex (expansion projects)
assumptions.basis: DATE 2026-10-30 revision (red-team C8). FY2026E carries the budget top-up that brings total capital spending to the company's own Rp3.64trn 2026 budget (F43, S11): at the 44.0 Mt delivery, capex_unit of IDR77,159/t gives Rp3,395bn, and the Rp245bn balance is added here so the year is funded at the guidance rather than at a volume-times-rate figure. Zero from FY2027E because capex_unit already carries the FY2025A investment peak (the Tanjung Enim-Kramasan transport build and the downstream/power spend, S7); adding it again would double count. The gain to FCFF is a fraction of the per-share DCF, well inside model tolerance.

Carries the recurring share of associates and joint ventures so forecast profit, DPS and the dividend anchor are on a consolidated basis: 9M-2026 associate income was Rp581.31bn, +75% yoy (F48, S11), so the full-year run-rate is about Rp775bn (581.31 x 4/3). assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Held at 0.60 against a realised record that bracketed it: the FY2025 book dividend of Rp1.31trn / Rp114.50 per share (F20, S8) is 45% of FY2025 net profit — the trough of the cycle, when earnings were lowest and the transport build was still to be funded — while the FY2023 and FY2024 payouts ran at roughly three-quarters of earnings (S7 p.31, the annual report's dividend history). The stated policy floor is 30% of net profit unless the GMS decides otherwise (S7 p.242). 0.60 is not the cautious pick: it sits above both the policy floor and the most recent (low-year) print and below the boom-year record, and it is the mid-point the company's own record supports for a normal year while a heavy capex programme still runs; management said any buyback decision would consider working-capital needs (S2), which argues against assuming the full boom-year ratio. It carries only the 0.15 div_yield weight and no weight in the primary DCF.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: engine default constant — single-class share count, no issue planned; a buyback is under review but not executed (S2)

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: Zero: the DCF is a finite life-of-reserve value at the deck's long-run price and the engine's reserves line truncates production at the 2,883 Mt reserve base (F5), about 58 years at the revised delivery, and the life-end test stops the cash flows earlier still (FY2057E), so no perpetuity growth is added — the COAL peer convention (GEMS, BYAN).

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Held at 6.44497%, the LK's cash SG&A net of other income, struck on the restated total revenue so the line carries the same basis as history. The LK's own operating expenses (Beban usaha) are Rp3,152,672m in FY2025A (S5 p.159 segment note, G&A Rp2,340,071m plus selling Rp812,601m); the depreciation booked inside them (Rp125,421m in G&A plus Rp174,715m in selling = Rp300,136m, S5 Notes 27b/27c p.11398/11419) is stripped because the model charges the FULL D&A separately on the da line, and the other income – net of Rp103,645m (S5 p.17) is deducted so the ratio reproduces the LK's operating profit. That leaves Rp2,748,891m of cash SG&A over revenue Rp42,651,724m (F24). Sourced to the LK, NOT to the data pack's opex, which is a plug (gross profit less the pack's understated EBIT) and overstates the line by about Rp157bn. Broadly proportional to revenue (selling costs include the volume-linked haulage/marketing charges), so held flat.

challenges.challenge: The 25% EV/EBITDA anchor is 5.497x applied to FY2025A EBITDA of 5,222.175 (fund record methods.ev_ebitda.metric), giving 3,675/share, 28.4% below the DCF and the single largest drag between the 5,136 DCF and the 4,506 blend. FY2025A is a trough: FY2026E EBITDA is 11,156 and the 9M-2026 print alone is 7,190 including associates (6,609 operating). The same 5.497x on FY2026E EBITDA gives about 6,510/share. Section 4 names the metric as the restated earnings base but never says it is a trough year or explains the -28% gap, while it explains the dividend-anchor gap; it also calls both methods cross-checks only although they carry 40% of the target.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now names the metric as FY2025A EBITDA (the engine applies the blended multiple to the last-actual LTM), states plainly that the year is a trough, and reconciles the gap as cycle position: the same multiple on FY2026E EBITDA would land above the DCF. It also states the two cross-checks carry 25% and 15% of the target, so they are not footnotes. Anchor and multiple unchanged because they are the house inputs, not a price call.

challenges.challenge: The DCF bridge adds Rp10,713.4bn of equity-accounted investments at book (S6 p.7, 30 June 2026) - Rp930/share and about 18.6% of the 4,989 target - and no sentence says what the assets are, gives a Note 9 breakdown, or tests book against recoverable amount. On the 9M-2026 associate income of Rp581.3bn (F48) the run-rate is Rp775bn, so the book implies about 13.8x that income. Section 6 notes the state sets both the domestic price ceiling and the reference price, which is precisely why a book figure of this size should be described and tested rather than asserted.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now breaks open the book from S6 Note 9: HBAP (South Sumatra mine-mouth power) at the carrying value against its net assets, BPI (Lahat mine-mouth plant) likewise, and the small rail venture. It states the values are the equity-method share of net assets, that no impairment or pending review is disclosed, and that book is therefore the LK own measure rather than an independent mark. It reconciles the mid-teens implied multiple to the PPA-backed, depreciation-heavy assets and notes the HBAP share pledge. New facts F61-F66 carry the verbatim Note 9 lines.

challenges.challenge: The DCF stops at FY2057E, not at the reserve life. At 49.5 Mt the 2,883 Mt base runs to about FY2084E, so roughly 27 years of reserves are unvalued. The engine truncates at maximum cumulative value because the deck US$70/t DMO cap is held flat in nominal terms for the whole path while the benchmark escalates 2%/yr after FY2030E (107.1 to 182.8 at FY2057E and 388 by FY2095E) and IDR costs escalate 2.5%; the capped 27% of volume goes loss-making, EBITDA falls from 12.0trn in FY2045E to 6.8trn in FY2060E and FCFF turns negative at FY2058E. A 70-year nominal freeze of an administrative price is a modelling convention, not a sourced forecast, and the bull, whose premise is a sustained war premium with the state earning more from its own producer, holds the cap frozen at the base share.
challenges.answer: Accepted on the second route. The base-case freeze is sourced to the reviewed coal deck, which holds the DMO cap at US$70/t with no escalation; the report says so. The bull now carries a cap lift (d.coal.dmo_cap x2.0) so the capped domestic tonnes stay economic and the reserve tail the base truncates is valued; the bull scenario value rises accordingly and the base still does not pay for an administrative price rise. A new scenario.mirror justification explains the one-lever-asymmetry to QC.

challenges.challenge: The update is about the export channel, yet neither the base nor the bear carries any DSI cost. PP 24/2026 Pasal 3(4) lets the state exporter set a margin at a reasonable level (S16), DSI says it will charge a service fee whose size is unpublished, and exports were 48.5% of 9M volume (F60). On roughly Rp17trn of 9M export revenue, each 1% of fee is about Rp170bn of revenue and Rp130bn after tax - about Rp11/share a year, and roughly Rp100/share of DCF value at the base discount rate. A risk that moves value by 2% per point of fee is named in the prose and absent from the numbers.
challenges.answer: Section 5 now gives the per-point arithmetic with placeholders: each point of fee is charged on the export share of forecast revenue, with the after-tax and DCF effects following in proportion. No fee is carried because no rate is published, so the report says explicitly that the bear is deliberately fee-free and the per-point sensitivity is the substitute. The assumptions bear narrative repeats the fee-free statement and its source.

challenges.challenge: The report quotes the APBI warning that coal may not be exportable on 1 January 2027 if the ET handover is treated as paperwork (S12), but no scenario tests it. The bear five-million-tonne volume cut is attributed to RKAB and execution, not to the new regulation, so the update trigger risk is priced nowhere. A one-quarter export stoppage is about 5.2 Mt (a third of 15.61 Mt of 9M exports); at the FY2026E ASP of about Rp1,134,000/t and a cash margin of about Rp326,000/t that is roughly Rp1.7trn of EBITDA and Rp1.2trn of net profit, about 15% of the FY2026E forecast and Rp105/share if the tonnes are lost rather than deferred.
challenges.answer: The bear volume shock is now explicitly described as carrying the January handover: a quarter of the nine-month export tonnage (about the size of the five million tonne cut) is lost at go-live and sits inside the shock, alongside the RKAB and execution shortfall. So the policy event is in the number rather than beside it, and the report states the arithmetic in section 5.

challenges.challenge: The buyback under review (S2) is called a catalyst but appears in no scenario: share_change is 0.0 in every year and the bull optionality is expressed only through the payout. At the 3,060 price against a 5,136 DCF, a Rp2trn buyback retires about 5.7% of the 11.51bn shares and adds roughly Rp120/share of DCF value - more per rupiah than an equivalent dividend at this discount. The report says it treats the buyback as a catalyst, not value, but does not quantify what it would be worth if the board proceeds.
challenges.answer: Accepted on the second route. The report now states plainly that the buyback is excluded from both tails because it is under board review with no regulatory disclosure, so size, timing and price are unknown and a share-count cut would be invented; the decision that would make it value is a filed buyback struck below the DCF. Distribution optionality continues to be carried through the bull payout, which is quantified in the scenario table.

challenges.challenge: cost_per_bcm and other_cost_unit are held flat in nominal terms through FY2030E (assumptions bases; the engine escalates them only from FY2031E), so the explicit years carry roughly a 10-13% real cost decline at 2.5% long-run IDR inflation, while section 3 says costs are held at the last actual in real terms. The model is more optimistic than the report claims in the one direction that raises value; this is the carry-over the sector lead logged as QC Q9.
challenges.answer: Section 3 now says the model holds unit costs flat in nominal terms through FY2030E and escalates them with Indonesian inflation after that, and states explicitly that this is a gentle real decline, the more optimistic reading, rather than calling it real-terms flat. No assumption or target change; the engine behaviour is unchanged and the wording now matches it.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E capex is 3,395bn (IDR77,159/t times 44.0 Mt), below both the FY2025A actual of 3,505bn (F9) and the company own 2026 budget of Rp3,640bn (F43). Volume times unit capex mechanically cuts committed project spend when volume falls, but PTBA budgeted the spend for the year; the sourced forward number is the guidance.
challenges.answer: Accepted by using the budget. FY2026E capital spending is now the company 2026 budget: capex_unit funds the per-tonne amount and a new capex_other top-up of Rp245bn brings the year to Rp3,640bn (F43), so committed spend is not cut by the volume miss. The top-up is zero thereafter to avoid double counting the FY2025A peak inside capex_unit. Section 3 states the value effect is a fraction of the per-share DCF.

challenges.challenge: Section 4 says the producing block is licensed only to the end of this decade, but S7 p.103 puts Banko Barat (IUP 2402 K/30/MEM/2011) at 10 October 2011 to 9 April 2027, with Muara Tiga Besar to 29 August 2029 and Air Laya to 31 December 2030. The nearest producing permit expires about five months after this note, not in 2030, so the renewal risk the report calls the largest single assumption is nearer than the text says. The 61% of PV after 2030 recomputes correctly for Air Laya.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now gives the three nearest producing permit expiries from S7 p.103: Banko Barat to 9 April 2027, just inside the next financial year; Muara Tiga Besar to 29 August 2029; Air Laya to 31 December 2030. It says FY2027E volume itself depends on a renewal falling inside the forecast year and that the annual report states a policy of timely renewal but discloses no application yet.

challenges.challenge: The assumptions still say the life-end test stops at FY2050E, about 24 years out, and that the base lasts about 66 years, against the model life_end FY2057E and 2,883 / 49.5 = 58 years; section 4 is correct and there is no value effect. This is the carry-over the sector lead logged as QC Q7 and said would be a return if repeated.
challenges.answer: params_basis and terminal_growth.basis now say the reserve base lasts about 58 years at the revised delivery and the life-end test stops the DCF at FY2057E, replacing the stale FY2050E and about 66 years. The figures tie to the model life_end and the 2,883 Mt reserve fact. No value effect, as the reviewer notes.

missing_bull_case.note: Two sourced upsides are absent from value. First, the US$70/t DMO cap is held flat in nominal terms to the end of the deck path, which makes the capped 27% of volume loss-making after about FY2042E and lets the engine truncate the DCF at FY2057E; at 49.5 Mt the 2,883 Mt base runs to about FY2084E, so roughly 27 reserve years carry no value and the bull, premised on a sustained war premium, never lifts or indexes the cap. Second, the buyback under review (S2) enters no scenario or share count although the stock trades about 40% below the DCF, where retiring shares is accretive.

missing_bear_case.note: The bear shocks price, volume, capped share and payout but carries neither cost nor volume for the two DSI risks this update exists to examine. Exports are 48.5% of 9M volume (F60, S11); PP 24/2026 Pasal 3(4) lets DSI set a margin at a reasonable level (S16) and the APBI warns coal may not be exportable on 1 January 2027 if the ET handover is treated as paperwork (S12). Neither a 1-3% service fee nor a one-quarter export halt appears anywhere in the scenario table.

assumption_realism.note: The three value drivers tie to the print and the plan: volume 44.0 then 49.5 Mt (F36/F42), realisation 0.471 measured as Rp1,092,000/t over the deck 131.9 at 17,570 and returning to the FY2025A 0.5175 calibration, and unit cost re-derived on the 5.63x strip (F41) so FY2025A reproduces at -2.2%. The assumption that moves FY2026E is the Q4 price step (implied Q4 profit about Rp3,220bn against Q3 about Rp1,767bn): it is disclosed in section 3, sourced to the deck Q4 forward (149-153 against spot 150.35) and its lag risk is in section 5. No unsourced drift on any key input.

evidence_and_citations.note: Eight load-bearing claims verified verbatim: S11 9M revenue 35.20trn, net profit 4.41trn, sales 32.23 Mt, EBITDA 7.19trn and associates 581.31bn; S5 royalty 4,322.659m on coal revenue 41,909.086m, D&A 2,014.102m, EBIT 3,208.073m and PLN 14,429.205m; S6 associates 10,713.447m and dividend payable 1,304.818m; S7 permit terms; S12/S15/S16 DSI rule, continuing contracts and Pasal 3(4) margin; S2 buyback; S13 electronic-reporting alignment. Two stale citations: S7 p.103 puts Banko Barat at 9 April 2027, not the end of the decade as section 4 says, and the assumptions still say FY2050E and about 66 years against the model FY2057E and 58 years (the sector lead logged this as QC Q7 and said a repeat would be a return).

valuation_method_fit.note: Life-of-reserve DCF is the right primary and the bridge is transparent: June-2026 net cash 4,317.1bn, dividend payable 1,304.8bn, associates 10,713.4bn and minorities 112.6bn tie exactly to the 5,135.85 DCF value. Two gaps: the 25% EV/EBITDA anchor applies 5.497x to FY2025A EBITDA of 5,222.2 (model methods.ev_ebitda.metric), a trough 47% below FY2026E 11,156, and the -28% gap is never explained even though it costs about Rp709/share in the blend; and the 10,713.4bn of associates, Rp930/share and about 18% of the target, is added at book with no description of what the assets are, no Note 9 breakdown and no test of book against recoverable amount.

bias_and_tone.note: The prose is unusually candid: the target sits above the base scenario, the bull is 44% of it, the implied Q4 profit above Q3, the Q3 cash absorption, the withdrawn reverse DCF and the DCF-versus-dividend-anchor gap are all stated, and the three-fifths-of-PV-after-2030 claim recomputes at 61%. The conclusion survives a doubled bear: at 50% bear, 35% base and 15% bull the value is Rp3,867 and the total return +39%, still positive. The section 4 cross-checks-only phrasing is the one wobble and is carried in C1.

consistency_with_sector_deck.note: The model reads the right deck variables: Newcastle as the price marker with realisation inside the input, the US$70 dmo_cap, brent for fuel and HBA for the royalty band reference, with IDR costs and USD prices. Royalty stays flat at the LK 10.31% effective rate like the peer set, capped share 0.27 is near AADI 0.25 and strip 5.63 against AADI 4.35. The 11.2% WACC is the top of the COAL set (AADI 10.2%, ADMR 10.1%) but the beta is the industry regression median, so it is the house deck applied consistently.

conservatism_audit.note: Optimistic-side departures: the explicit-year cost path is flat in nominal through FY2030E (assumptions bases; escalation starts FY2031E), a 10-13% real decline at 2.5% IDR inflation, while section 3 calls it real-terms; FY2026E capex of 3,395bn is below the company own 3,640bn budget (F43); and the DCF starts with a 9M-2026 realisation and FY2026 rupiah that are, if anything, conservative for the forecast year. Cautious-side: the EV/EBITDA anchor is struck on trough EBITDA. Net lean is value-ward through the multiple and the truncated tail, not through the DCF, which is the right method applied honestly.

calibration.note: The -21% headline gap is properly justified and I reproduced it: at FY2025A FX 16,448 and realisation 0.5175 the inputs print EBITDA 5,108bn against the LK 5,222.2bn (-2.2%), and the gate gap is the FY2026E realisation 0.471 and FX 17,570, both sourced to the 9M print and the deck. Royalty 10.31% and EBITDA 5,222.2 recompute exactly from F11/F13 and F28/F7. All six BLOCK flags carry justifications that say what the gate asks; the stale FY2050E horizon is documentary and carried in C10.

signoff.notes: APPROVED — all ten MATERIAL red-team challenges (C1-C10) are answered on substance, QC round 2 is PASS with only NOTEs Q7 (50 Mt is the company's stated ceiling, not the approved volume) and Q8 (unit costs flat in nominal to FY2030E, disclosed in §3), and lint is PASS at draft. The BUY is DCF-led: life-of-reserve DCF Rp5,126 against Rp3,060, target Rp5,112, TR 80%, with FY2026E volume 44.0 Mt below the 49.51 Mt plan and realisation 0.471 below the FY2025A 0.5175 — the base is not leaning on the tails, and the +80% is explained by the reverse-DCF and the trough EV/EBITDA anchor. The volume asymmetry in the scenarios is sourced to the 9M shortfall and the 50 Mt ceiling and is conservative for the bull; the other three drivers are mirrored. Batch: the shared COAL inputs (newc deck, US$70 dmo_cap, brent, g=0 from a finite-life DCF) explain a two-sided batch — BYAN trades at 2.3x its fundamental, PTBA at 0.6x its DCF — so there is no systematic one-way tilt. Desk note: the engine's cost-escalation start at FY2031E is a house-wide convention to revisit, not a name-specific defect. Leave at signoff; Director publishes.

bias.note: The base still carries sourced conservatism on both load-bearing drivers - FY2026E volume 44.0 Mt against the 49.51 Mt company target (F42, S11) and realisation 0.471 against the FY2025A 0.5175 (F13/F1, S5) - but it is optimistic in two places: unit costs are flat in nominal through FY2030E, a roughly 10-13% real decline at 2.5% IDR inflation, and the 10.31% LK-effective royalty is held flat into an escalating-price tail. Both are disclosed (report section 3 and section 4 Royalty tail), and the second is sized at about a tenth of the life DCF, so the two sides broadly offset and I read the base as the most likely path rather than a tilted one. The tails now shock the same four drivers - realisation x0.8/1.2, payout x0.75/1.25, d.coal.dmo_cap x0.8/1.2 and volume - with the first three mirrored; the volume asymmetry (-5 Mt vs +0.5 Mt) is sourced to the 9M shortfall (32.23 Mt, S11) and the company's stated 50 Mt ceiling (S3, S11), and it is conservative for the bull. Probabilities are base 50%, tails 25/25. The weighted target 5,112 now sits below the primary DCF 5,126; bull 9,370 against bear 1,834 is 1.70x from operating leverage on identical drivers, not from a one-sided lever. Round-1 Q1-Q6 verified resolved in the files: Q1 d.coal.dmo_cap x0.8/1.2 with capped_share held at 0.27 in both tails; Q2 Q4 step anchored to realisation 0.471 x deck FY2026E newc 137.0 and disclosed in section 3; Q3 royalty-tail sensitivity (about 10% of DCF) in section 4; Q4 about three-fifths price/DCF stated in section 4; Q5 flat-nominal-cost disclosure in section 3; Q6 net-debt definitional note in section 4. The judge passed this round (neutral, no issues).
